title: Migrating 7-Year Legacy ERP to Medallion Data Warehouse with CDC & Zero Data Loss
summary: Extracting MySQL binlogs via Change Data Capture, implementing idempotent Go workers on RabbitMQ, and cutting analytics query latency by 70% with zero downtime.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.business-data-requirements: An ERP system running for 7 years accumulated massive retail transactions. The Business Intelligence (BI) and executive teams required hourly near-real-time reports. However, the legacy OLTP MySQL database with bloated Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) tables suffered 100% CPU spikes during heavy reporting queries.
sections.data-modeling:
We decoupled OLAP from OLTP by implementing a Medallion Architecture (Data Lakehouse) on PostgreSQL/ClickHouse:

  • Bronze Tier (Raw Ingestion): Append-only tables preserving original JSON event payloads extracted from MySQL binlogs.
  • Silver Tier (Cleaned & Conformed): Normalized Third Normal Form (3NF) models with sanitized types and foreign key relationships.
  • Gold Tier (Dimensional Star Schema): Fact tables for sales/inventory and Dimension tables for customers and products optimized for BI tools.
sections.pipeline-construction:
The CDC pipeline operated non-intrusively without touching legacy ERP application code:

  • Binary Log Ingestion (CDC): Debezium/Canal listening to MySQL row-based binlogs and dispatching events to RabbitMQ.
  • Idempotent Go Workers: High-concurrency Golang workers consuming queue messages and executing upserts with ON CONFLICT (id, version) DO UPDATE.
  • Dead Letter Exchange (DLX): Corrupted records or network failures routed to retry queues with exponential backoff.
sections.testing-optimization:
Verification and performance tuning included:

  • Data Reconciliation: Automated nightly checksum and row count validation between MySQL OLTP and PostgreSQL Warehouse.
  • Tuning: Monthly table partitioning, BRIN indexes on query timestamps, and micro-batching writes at 500 records per transaction.
  • End-to-End Latency: Transaction commit to warehouse availability reduced to under 1.8 seconds.
sections.summary-recommendations: Achieved 96% data reconciliation accuracy with 0% data loss and slashed analytics query execution time by 70%. Recommendation: Always enforce Idempotency Keys and Schema Registries from day one.

title: High-Throughput Event Ingestion Architecture with Spring WebFlux, Kafka & Automated PII Anonymization
summary: Building a privacy-compliant MarTech ingestion gateway handling tens of thousands of real-time e-commerce events per second with sub-second latency.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.context-problem: During peak e-commerce promotional events, user traffic surges 15-20x. The tracking gateway must ingest tens of thousands of micro-events/sec (cart adds, product views, checkout clicks) for real-time dispatch to Google Analytics 4 and Facebook Conversions API without degrading user browsing performance.
sections.system-requirements:
• Functional: Real-time ingestion, validation, categorization, and dispatch to downstream ad-tech platforms.
  • Non-Functional: p99 API latency < 15ms, throughput capacity of 10,000 RPS, automated PII sanitization, and zero data loss on third-party outages.
sections.architecture-design:
Designed as a non-blocking Reactive Event-Driven pipeline:

  • Ingestion Layer: Spring WebFlux (Project Reactor + Netty) receiving asynchronous HTTP requests and streaming directly to Apache Kafka clusters.
  • Privacy & Sanitization: Spring AOP and custom Jackson serializers recursively detecting sensitive fields (emails, phones, IDs) and applying Salted SHA-256 hashing before outbound dispatch.
  • Outbox & Delivery: Kafka worker services consuming events and communicating with external APIs via non-blocking WebClient.
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Comparing Synchronous vs Reactive architectures:

  • Synchronous (Spring MVC + Tomcat): Straightforward debugging, but thread-per-request model leads to thread exhaustion under 5,000 concurrent connections.
  • Reactive Non-Blocking (Spring WebFlux): Steeper learning curve for stream operations and backpressure management, but sustains 20,000+ RPS stably on minimal CPU cores with 60% lower RAM utilization.
sections.lessons-best-practices: Integrate Resilience4j Circuit Breakers and exponential backoff retries at the outbound gateway layer. Never perform blocking I/O operations on WebFlux event loop threads.

title: Optimizing Multi-Stage Docker (<25MB) & Building Zero-Downtime CI/CD Pipeline with GitHub Actions
summary: Lightweight Alpine packaging strategies, Nginx SPA fallback configurations, and automated static typechecks in continuous release pipelines.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.article-objectives: Guide to building ultra-lightweight SPA web container images (< 25MB) using Docker Multi-Stage Builds on Alpine Linux, coupled with automated GitHub Actions CI/CD for Zero-Downtime Deployments.
sections.architecture-principles:
Two distinct deployment stages:

  • Stage 1 (Builder): node:20-alpine image installs dependencies, executes linting/typechecking, and produces optimized static assets in /dist.
  • Stage 2 (Production Runner): Only the compiled /dist folder is copied into nginx:alpine-slim (< 15MB) with gzip compression and secure HTTP headers.
  • GitHub Actions Pipeline: Automatically triggered on PR/Push to main: Lint -> Test -> Build -> Docker Push -> Deploy.
sections.step-by-step-setup:
Configuration details:

  • Step 1: Multi-stage Dockerfile with non-root user and .dockerignore excluding node_modules and extraneous docs.
  • Step 2: nginx.conf configured with try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; and static cache headers.
  • Step 3: Workflow .github/workflows/deploy.yml leveraging Docker Buildx cache to speed up CI runs by 3x.
sections.troubleshooting-pitfalls:
• 404 on page refresh in SPA: Missing Nginx fallback to index.html. Resolved with try_files directive.
  • Bloated images: Caused by copying devDependencies into the final image without multi-stage builds.
  • Security risks: Running containers as root. Fixed by specifying USER nginx.
sections.evaluation-scaling: Reduced Docker image size from 850MB to 22MB and deployment time from 6 minutes to under 45 seconds. Future roadmap: Integrate Trivy container vulnerability scanning and Kubernetes canary rollouts.

title: Building High-Performance Concurrent Worker Pool in Golang with Context & Graceful Shutdown
summary: Bounded concurrent job queue pattern using fixed goroutines, context.Context timeout control, and graceful OS signal handling.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement: When processing millions of database I/O records or dispatching batch email notifications, spawning an unbounded goroutine per task (go processTask(t)) rapidly causes out-of-memory crashes and database connection pool exhaustion.
sections.initial-approach: Initial naive implementations often rely on sync.WaitGroup across unbounded goroutines. Under a spike of 50,000 tasks, the server consumes multiple Gigabytes of memory and the database rejects connection requests.
sections.optimization-thinking:
Designed a Bounded Concurrency Worker Pool:

  • Buffered channels act as task queues to prevent memory bloat.
  • Fixed N worker goroutines continuously listen on the task channel.
  • context.WithCancel or context.WithTimeout enables graceful task abortion on long-running timeouts.
sections.code-implementation:
Implemented a WorkerPool struct managing channels and graceful shutdown:

type WorkerPool struct {
  workers int
  tasks   chan Task
  wg      sync.WaitGroup
  ctx     context.Context
  cancel  context.CancelFunc
}

Upon receiving SIGTERM, the pool closes the task channel and waits for active workers to finish pending work before exiting.
sections.complexity-applications: Maintains fixed O(N) memory complexity relative to worker count, sustaining 8,000 tasks/sec throughput under 50MB RAM. Widely applicable in data ingestion, batch ETL, and webhook dispatch engines.
